item.title: Democrats may have an unlikely ally in a post-midterms effort to oust Hegseth
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Senate Democrats are quietly floating the ouster of Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth after the Nov. 3 election as the political price for cooperation on key defense-related issues in the postelection lame-duck session, and they may have some GOP support to shake up the Pentagon’s leadership, according to Senate sources. The Defense Department has set recruiting records under Hegseth’s leadership, and the Pentagon chief appears to have strong support from President Trump, who likes to brag that Hegseth looks like a military leader from “central casting.” But some Republican senators haven’t been happy with Hegseth’s leadership, especially his ouster of well-respected military leaders such as Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, Army chief of staff Randy George, Navy Secretary John Phelan and four-star Gen. Chris Donahue, the top U.S. military officer in Europe. Democrats view Hegseth’s leadership as a disaster and are looking for leverage to push him out after the midterm elections, according to Senate sources, just as they attempted to push former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem out of her job during the prolonged stalemate over funding for her department earlier this year. Trump eventually fired Noem after key Republican senators, such as Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), turned against her publicly. Now Democrats have significant leverage over Hegseth’s future at the Pentagon as they’re threatening to hold up emergency defense funding the White House requested in June as well as regular funding for the Defense Department, which expires on Dec. 11. Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hegseth’s resignation could set the stage for more bipartisan cooperation on must-pass defense bills, such as the National Defense Authorization Act and the annual defense appropriations bill. Kaine told The Hill before the Senate adjourned for the election that Hegseth’s departure would help lower the partisan temperature in the standoff over the defense measures. Republican sources say that Senate Democrats have already privately floated Hegseth’s termination as something that could help muster bipartisan cooperation on filling key vacancies at the Pentagon, such as the positions of Army and Navy secretary left open by the departures of Driscoll and Phelan. As things now stand, Senate Democrats are threatening to block the defense spending bills and also a waiver for Hung Cao, Trump’s nominee to serve as Navy secretary. Cao needs a special congressional waiver to lead the Navy because federal law requires a seven-year waiting period before former military officers can be confirmed to top Pentagon civilian leadership posts. Democrats are drawing a hard line on supporting defense funding in the lame-duck session if the military conflict with Iran isn’t wrapped up before the end of the year. “My own view is that if the war is over, then the opportunity for bipartisanship on defense authorization and defense appropriations is there. I think if the war’s not over, it’s going to be extremely difficult,” said Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), who is poised to take over as Democratic whip in the next Congress. Schatz said he was speaking about his personal view of the prospects of a deal on defense spending. So far, some key Senate Republicans say they don’t see Trump agreeing to push Hegseth out of the job to get cooperation from Democrats on the defense authorization and funding measures in the lame-duck session. “That’s a bridge too far,” warned a GOP senator, who requested anonymity to discuss the looming negotiations over breaking the logjam on defense legislation after Election Day. A senior Pentagon official dismissed the criticism of Hegseth’s leadership from Democrats and some key Republicans by pointing to his record of accomplishments over the past 20 months. “Secretary Hegseth has been a transformative leader for the Department of War and, at President Trump’s direction, has ushered in a new era of Peace Through Strength,” the official said in response to jockeying by Democrats to push Hegseth out of his role, using the Trump administration's preferred name for the Department of Defense. “Standards and merit are back, our arsenal is stronger than ever before, and morale and recruitment across every service are at all-time highs. Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way. By every measurable metric, the Department of War is better under Secretary Hegseth’s leadership than before,” the senior official said. “The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first.” There are growing questions, however, on Capitol Hill about whether Trump and Hegseth are fully in sync on several important issues. Trump recently cancelled Hegseth’s plan to run a livestream of the execution of Maj. Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 at a mass shooting at Fort Hood in 2009. There’s also confusion about whether Hegseth or other senior Pentagon officials directed a temporary halt to intelligence sharing with Ukraine or ordered the restriction of Ukraine’s access to the Starshield satellite-based internet network, without Trump’s knowledge and approval. Four Republican senators — Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (Maine), Sen. John Cornyn (Texas), Sen. Thom Tillis (N.C.) and Sen. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) — signed a bipartisan letter last week directing the Defense Department inspector general, Platte Moring, demanding he immediately investigate whether any Pentagon officials “directed” or “authorized” changes to intelligence-sharing arrangements or Starlink and Starshield services affecting Ukraine. Collins has separately faulted Hegseth for not fully anticipating that Iran would be able to shut down most shipping traffic, including nearly a quarter of the world’s seaborne oil supply, through the vulnerable Strait of Hormuz in response to U.S. and Israeli attacks. “For example, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz should have been anticipated. It happened during the Iraq-Iran war and it’s an obvious point of leverage but there doesn’t seem to have been any plan for it,” Collins said last month. Tillis wrote in his new memoir that his decision to cast a deciding vote to confirm Hegseth in January 2025 is “the biggest regret of my career.” Some Republicans already acknowledge that pushing Hegseth out of his job in the lame-duck session could avoid a messy impeachment battle next year, aside from paving the way for a potential deal on the defense authorization and appropriations bills before Christmas. “Trump should fire Hegseth to avoid Hegseth’s impeachment. It’s the honorable thing to do,” Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) posted Thursday on the social platform X. The maverick conservative who lost his primary reelection bid earlier this year when Trump endorsed his opponent noted that Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) had to scramble to avoid voting on Hegseth’s impeachment before the election. “The House recessed early to avoid the vote, so I will reintroduce Hegseth articles of impeachment when we return for the lame duck session, regardless of the outcome of the midterm election,” House Democrats, led by Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.), filed six articles of impeachment against Hegseth in April. Democrats in the lower chamber plan to make Hegseth a top political target next year if they win the majority in next month’s election, something that political handicappers project is likely. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) told Semafor that impeaching Hegseth should be one of House Democrats’ “top three priorities” next year. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. item.title: Republicans already know who they want to blame if they suffer big midterm losses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republicans are already starting to blame each other as the midterm election spirals further out of their control. Everyone is bracing for President Donald Trump's ire if the party loses big in November. House Republicans are planning to accuse the Senate side. Trump political aides have taken to directly calling campaigns they feel aren't performing well enough. National GOP operatives are quietly furious at lackluster candidates who didn't do enough to prepare for a tough year despite early warnings. And some GOP candidates are pointing the finger back at their own party committees. It's a vicious cycle, according to more than a dozen top GOP operatives and lawmakers who spoke to POLITICO, some of whom were granted anonymity to candidly discuss private conversations. “If it happens, there will be plenty of blame to go around,” said Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R-N.J.), who is in his own tighter-than-comfortable race. That Republicans have already spent significant time gaming out the aftermath and how to insulate themselves from the fallout of what they fear will be significant GOP losses illustrates how precarious the current landscape is for the party. That’s even as top Republicans publicly insist they are bullish on keeping control of both chambers in Congress. Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), who is widely expected to be the next National Republican Senatorial Committee chair, told reporters Thursday that “if the Democrats do win the House and the Senate, it won't be because of their left-wing lunatic candidates, it'll be because people are pissed off about gas prices, and I get that.” House Republicans are annoyed with Senate Republicans for fumbling a once-safe GOP map as well as creating top-of-the-ticket drag for them with bad candidates in some key states — but senators privately put the onus on Trump for forcing out better Republican incumbents and then backing flawed GOP candidates, including Ken Paxton in Texas , according to three GOP senators and a national GOP operative. The top Senate GOP Super PAC and Trump’s MAGA Inc. have spent nearly $200 million alone to save Paxton, who’s locked in a tight race with Democrat James Talarico. Trump, for his part, has already landed on who to blame in the event of a Paxton loss next month. “If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday afternoon , targeting the Texas senator he endorsed against in the primary in Cornyn, and a longtime GOP foe in Rove. There’s also particular frustration with Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), who numerous GOP operatives grumbled never took his race seriously and is now costing the party millions of dollars to rescue in a state Democrats haven’t won in almost a century. Marshall’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. “No one in the world expected that the Senate would need as much money as they did,” said one national GOP operative working on multiple competitive House races. “All of this money that was expected to go to the House, for the most part, is now being wasted on the Senate because they fucked up so bad.” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle blasted “armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation” and said Trump “is laser-focused on maintaining Republican majorities in Congress this November, which is why he is traveling across the country highlighting the historic victories his Administration has delivered for the American people.” “The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction,” Ingle said. “Those who are actually involved with Republicans' midterm strategy remain laser-focused on winning races and are confident we are still in a position to protect and expand our majorities," said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre. A slew of troubling internal GOP polling in recent weeks set off a new level of panic across House GOP leadership, political operations and individual campaigns. It didn’t just reveal a harsh environment for the party in power on par with typical midterms, but potentially catastrophic scenarios in formerly safe red seats across the country. Even top House Republicans expect to lose the House majority at this point. A growing group of Hill Republicans argue the blame rests with Trump, and his decisions to get the U.S. into an open-ended war with Iran that has driven up fuel prices, while enacting a slew of tariffs and other policy moves that have riled farmers. “I’ve talked to some who are making these decisions: The biggest problem is the president’s polling numbers and unfavorables,” retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) recently told POLITICO . Still, not everyone is blaming Trump: In an explosive move this week, GOP Rep. Anna Paulina Luna of Florida, who is close with the president and faces her own surprisingly competitive race, accused the National Republican Congressional Committee of dropping the ball. “I am also getting calls from members wondering what is going on at the @NRCC,” Luna posted on social media , adding she was also getting inquiries about House leadership races. “Sounds to me like some in leadership need to focus on winning races instead of gaming their next steak donor dinner.” (The post has since been deleted.) Some rank-and-file Republicans are frustrated the NRCC didn’t pivot faster to trying to shore up at-risk GOP incumbents across the map as the landscape deteriorated in August and September. “The leadership at the NRCC is living in a bubble,” another House Republican said. “We’re getting killed out here.” Mike Marinella, a spokesperson for the NRCC, noted that the committee moved early to launch coordinated advertising campaigns with incumbents in districts not initially rated as competitive, including those represented by Reps. Jeff Hurd (R-Colo.), Bill Huizenga (R-Mich.), Rob Wittman (R-Va.), Mike Turner (R-Ohio), and Monica De La Cruz (R-Texas). To date, the NRCC has run coordinated advertising in 51 districts, Marinella said. GOP lawmakers and operatives working to defend the party’s majorities in Congress have been discussing amongst themselves how to avoid being thrown under the bus come Nov. 3, according to a dozen of the people interviewed. The rising tensions have also turned up in the rather intense shadow leadership race underway within Speaker Mike Johnson’s circle and the senior ranks of the House GOP, with opposing camps preparing to blame each other, according to five of the people. GOP Whip Tom Emmer has said publicly that some of the GOP redistricting efforts won’t work, and Republicans won’t win all those seats. Trump officials have also been feeling the pressure, sometimes calling campaigns to try to revive lagging operations or attempting to install new staff within them, according to two Republicans familiar with the matter. In another stunning move, Trump officials are warning Republicans that pro-Trump super PACs can only help so much and the candidates need to shift their strategy to a positive message and a list of key deliverables for voters — or they will lose. “Republican success in many cases is going to hinge on the following: do they give voters a reason to vote for them?” a senior Republican official familiar with MAGA Inc.’s plans said. “They're being inundated with reasons to vote against the Democrats, and in many places they already instinctually want to. But are they given a reason to actually vote for the Republicans to show up and vote?” The person added that “the number one thing that every Republican in the country” should be doing in the final weeks is laying out “things that they are going to do to tangibly improve people's personal economic situation and their life” and “lower your cost of living.” “If Republicans are failing to lay out a reason to come vote for them and saying, ‘Here's what I, as a candidate, am for, what I am going to do to make your economics better,’ there’s a good chance they're going to lose,” the Republican official warned. That assessment has shocked several Republicans in tough races. It’s a big shift from even how House leadership has approached the campaign trail: Johnson has spent the last few weeks hammering a message of contrast between his party of “common sense” and Democrats as a party of dangerous socialists who will investigate the president and empower America’s “enemies” if they win. “We’re running for our lives,” another House Republican in a tough race said. “Those are two totally different approaches. And we have two weeks.” Erin Doherty contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/republican-knives-out-midterms-trump-01124859

item.title: France imposes curfews after violent protests lead to thousands of arrests
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Sudip Kar-Gupta and Elizabeth Pineau PARIS, Oct 19 (Reuters) - French authorities set curfews in parts of several cities on Monday, including Paris, Lille and Nice, as they faced pressure over security failings after a weekend of riots and looting stemming from nationwide anti-government protests. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu had ruled out a blanket curfew in Paris but not a state of emergency, and had said ‌it was more appropriate for now to apply partial and localised curfews. "My determination to restore order is absolute," he told reporters. Paris police said they had issued orders barring protests in certain areas of ‌the French capital from 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) and had issued a curfew around the Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11:00 p.m. Both would remain in effect until 6 a.m. on Tuesday morning. "A police deployment is in place to ensure strict compliance with these measures," ​the police said in a statement. A source in Lecornu's office said a curfew for minors had been set between 8 p.m. and 6 a.m. for the next two days in Lille, Douai, Wattignies and Denain with the agreement of the local mayors. In Nice, mayor Eric Ciotti said in a video posted online that he had signed an order installing a curfew for minors in central Nice overnight. Marseille banned gatherings and demonstrations. French unions meanwhile called for a new round of strikes and rallies on November 5. The weekend of looting and violence between some protesters and police followed weeks of student demonstrations, rocking France six months ahead of its next presidential election and highlighting pressures from a weak economy and surging debt. MINISTER ‌BLAMES FAR LEFT Lecornu blamed far-left groups for some of France's worst unrest in ⁠years. "There is, after all, a far-left movement that wants to cause — we can't put it any more strongly — profound unrest in the country in the run-up to the presidential election," he said. Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon urged him to provide evidence. "Otherwise, he should apologise, keep quiet and stop fanning the flames of unrest," he said on X. The Federation of Trade ⁠and Retail said almost 3,000 shops had been affected over the weekend. "Behind every ransacked shop are business owners, employees and families who have seen years of work and effort wiped out in a matter of hours," it added, calling for social security and tax relief for affected businesses. Lecornu said the government would provide furlough measures from Tuesday. Standing before a boarded-up shopfront, Gerard Nouchi, manager of two clothing stores in Marseille, said there weren't enough police to stop the looters. "They trashed everything, broke things, insulted ​us," ​Nouchi said. "It was like a real tornado." The government ordered platforms selling looted goods to take down announcements and collaborate to prosecute ​resellers, Junior Digital Minister Anne Le Hénanff wrote on X. Some 2,400 people were arrested and ‌one protester died from a cardiac arrest on Saturday while nearly 1,000 officers were injured, according to the Interior Ministry. 'LEFT WITHOUT PROTECTION' French assets were underperforming broader European markets on Monday, though moves were more contained than at some other moments of recent political friction. Tensions in President Emmanuel Macron's fragile government over apparent security shortcomings — coming as the government needs to pass a budget bill to rein in its finances — could further unsettle investors. Macron's office said on Monday he had turned down his Interior Minister Laurent Nunez's offer to resign, telling him instead to put an end to barricades and looting and be transparent over what Macron called "intelligence and foresight failings". Nunez told reporters that Tuesday evening's Champions League soccer match between Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona would go ahead as planned. The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon said in a joint op-ed in the newspaper Liberation that they were used to demonstrations and protests. "But on Saturday ... ‌for the first time, we had the feeling that whole sections of our cities had been left without protection," said the ​mayors, all from the centre-left. The start of school holidays on Monday may provide relief, but students were staging more gatherings and blockades in some places, ​including the Louvre gallery and Sciences Po university in central Paris. LUXURY BOUTIQUES DAMAGED At the weekend, hundreds of thousands ​took to the streets to protest over what many say are declining and dysfunctional public services. At the Place Vendome in Paris, home to luxury hotels and boutiques, most shops were shuttered ‌and surrounded by security guards on Monday. The front door of a Dior boutique was ​smashed, while windows belonging to other luxury brand stores in ​central Paris, including Rolex, Louis Vuitton, Ralph Lauren and Gucci, were damaged. item.title: With the midterms just weeks away, the battle for Congress is coming into focus
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The 2026 midterm elections are just two weeks away. So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to geek out over some cold, hard data. The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. Big events can, and often do, change the course of elections. Yet the stakes in November couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too. The state-by-state midterm landscape is finally taking shape — and a few clear polling trends are emerging. Here are the numbers to watch as Election Day nears. The generic congressional ballot Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds). You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading. History is helpful here, courtesy of the RealClear Politics polling average : At this point in 2022 — after more than a year and a half of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Republicans had a small but significant lead (2.4 percentage points) on the generic ballot. Two weeks later, the GOP translated its final polling lead of 3 percentage points into nine seats — enough to flip the House . At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 7.7 points on the generic ballot. Two weeks later, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House . Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But two weeks out, voters had clearly broken against Democrats. In 2014, a final Republican polling lead of 2.4 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House ; in 2010, those numbers were 9.4 points and 63 seats, respectively . So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot — about 9 percentage points , on average — and it has been steadily growing over the last month. Democrats might not reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with . But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House. Advantage? Democrats. 12 specific Senate races National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible. In the states where Dems are playing defense — Michigan, Georgia, New Hampshire — their leads are solidifying; meanwhile, red states such as Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and South Carolina seem increasingly competitive. Here are the 12 races to follow: Maine (Republican seat) Republican Susan Collins (incumbent) Democrat Troy Jackson What the latest polls say : Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner , the Democrats' previous scandal-plagued nominee, tends to lead Collins by anywhere from 2 to 4 percentage points . One recent poll shows a tie. Michigan (Democratic seat) Republican Mike Rogers (former member of Congress) Democrat Abdul El-Sayed (public-health epidemiologist and former Wayne County, Mich. health director) What the latest polls say : Twenty polls have been conducted over the last month. Eighteen of them showed El-Sayed in the lead, by anywhere from 1 to 7 percentage points . Ohio (Republican seat) Republican Jon Husted (incumbent) Democrat Sherrod Brown (former senator) What the latest polls say : All but one poll conducted over the last month shows Brown leading Husted , with margins ranging from 1 to 8 percentage points. Georgia (Democratic seat) Democrat Jon Ossoff (incumbent) Republican Mike Collins (member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Ossoff holds a solid lead over Collins, with October polls putting him ahead by an average of 8 percentage points . North Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Michael Whatley (former Republican National Committee chairman) Democrat Roy Cooper (former governor) What the latest polls say : Cooper leads by nearly 10 points, on average . The most recent survey showed him ahead by 14 . New Hampshire (Democratic seat) Republican John E. Sununu (former U.S. senator) Democrat Chris Pappas (four-term U.S. representative) What the latest polls say: Pappas and Sununu were previously trading leads in polls in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. But Pappas appears to have opened a substantial lead — average margin: 7 percentage points — over the last month. Alaska (Republican seat) Republican Dan Sullivan (incumbent) Democrat Mary Peltola (former member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Surveys conducted in October show Peltola leading by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . But some September polls showed a tie, or Sullivan slightly ahead. Iowa (Republican seat) Republican Ashley Hinson (member of Congress) Democrat Josh Turek (state legislator and former Paralympic athlete) What the latest polls say : Hinson and Turek have traded small leads in surveys released since Iowa's June 2 primaries . Texas (Republican seat) Republican Ken Paxton (state attorney general) Democrat James Talarico (state legislator) What the latest polls say : Nearly every poll conducted over the summer has shown Talarico leading Paxton, though the margins are small — between 1 and 6 points. Nebraska (Republican seat) Republican Pete Ricketts (incumbent and former governor) Independent Dan Osborn (veteran and former union leader with Democratic support) What the latest polls say : Surveys are few and far between. But the most recent results suggest Osborn could be competitive. Kansas (Republican seat) Republican Roger Marshall (incumbent) Democrat Adam Hamilton (Methodist pastor who previously considered an independent run) What the latest polls say : Marshall leads by 1 point in the most recent sounding — but that is the only survey conducted over the last month that shows him ahead. The rest (save one tie) give Hamilton a slight edge (between 1 and 5 percentage points). South Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Darline Graham (incumbent, appointed to replace her brother Lindsey Graham after his death in July) Democrat Annie Andrews (pediatrcian and former U.S. House candidate) What the latest polls say : Graham holds a narrow lead in recent surveys . But it is small enough — between 1 and 3 percentage points — that Democrats are now targeting South Carolina as well. Advantage? Democrats. They’ve been consistently gaining ground over the last month, to the point where they are now favored to flip the Senate — unless the polls are wrong. Trump's approval rating — especially on affordability To one degree or another, midterm elections are always referendums on how the president is performing. So Trump is the final piece of the puzzle. At the moment, that's unfortunate news for Republicans on Capitol Hill and those looking to join them. According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , 60% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 38% who approve. That puts the president's net disapproval rating at 22%. Again, history can provide perspective . In mid-September 2018, Trump was about 12 points "underwater"; Republicans went on to lose 41 seats that November. Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top 2026 issue: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today, 73% disapprove and 24% approve. That's a 49-point gap. In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection. Advantage? Democrats. item.title: Zelensky briefs U.S. lawmakers and raises concerns about delay in air-defense interceptors
item.description:

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with a bipartisan group of lawmakers on Monday and raised concerns about President Donald Trump’s decision to waive key sanctions on Russia, as members of Congress push back against the president’s moves to ease economic pressure on Moscow. During the video call, Zelenskyy reported concerns over disruptions to U.S. intelligence sharing and the administration’s decision to waive Russia sanctions. He also told lawmakers that critical Starlink services remained degraded, hindering Ukraine’s ability to intercept drones from Moscow, according to a readout from Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.). Blumenthal and Tillis led the meeting, which included members of both the House and the Senate. “Funding Russia’s war machine, disabling Ukraine’s satellite communications, and crippling its air defense are all impediments to peace,” the senators wrote in a joint statement. “Trying to appease a murderous thug like Vladimir Putin will only prolong this war and bring greater casualties.” According to the readout, Zelenskyy also raised concerns about delays in the delivery of critical air-defense interceptors. “As a result of these disruptions, civilians — children — are dying,” Blumenthal and Tillis said. In his own social media post , Zelenskyy reiterated what he told lawmakers and said he has received “no explanation" from America on intelligence sharing and Starlink degradation. “Without America, things would be much harder for us,” Zelenskyy told lawmakers in the video. The call comes days after Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions on Russia that were outlined in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act — which he signed last month — that was intended to pressure Moscow to end the war. Trump also temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel earlier this month, in the president’s latest effort to bring down prices ahead of the midterms. That decision drew bipartisan criticism, including from Blumenthal and Tillis, who joined other senators in calling for Trump to “immediately reverse course.” Zelenskyy also told lawmakers that he was willing to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities, as Trump has proposed , if Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to do the same, the senators said. Speaking to reporters at the White House Monday, Trump defended his sanctions relief and accused Zelenskyy of standing in the way of ending the war. "I'm supporting stopping war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said when asked about criticism that he was supporting Putin. "And frankly, Zelenskyy is not helping matter much. I think he doesn't want to stop it." Trump also said he would be willing to meet with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping without Zelenskyy to discuss ending the war, and suggested someone else should negotiate for Ukraine. "Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said when asked about the Ukrainian leader's criticism that he was on the wrong side of history. "Maybe it's time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate." When ask for comment, the White House pointed back to the president's remarks. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), who also participated in the meeting, said he assured Zelenskyy of Congress’ continued support and stressed that Ukraine must be included in negotiations over its future. “While Trump’s oil handouts to Vladimir Putin undermine the war effort, I made clear on our call that Congress is determined to support the brave Ukrainian people in their fight for freedom,” Durbin said. “Any negotiations about the future of Ukraine after years defending against Russian assault must include Ukraine.” Jordain Carney contributed to this report. item.title: Feds charge 28 alleged noncitizen voters in California as election fight escalates
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Homeland Security Investigations task force officers escort a suspect accused of illegally registering to vote during a federal operation Monday in Commerce. (Jae C. Hong / Associated Press) Federal authorities have charged 28 people from across California with illegally registering to vote or casting ballots in federal elections despite not being U.S. citizens — again escalating an election battle between the state and the Trump administration just weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms. Authorities said 11 of the 28 were arrested as of Monday morning and that the 17 others “will be in custody in the near future.” Some of the 28, all of whom are lawful permanent residents of the U.S., are charged with lying about registering or voting on their naturalization paperwork, officials said; 21 of them are suspected of casting votes, some in multiple elections. None are undocumented immigrants, a favorite target of President Trump and a group he has accused of infiltrating U.S. elections in the past. Those charged represent a tiny fraction of the 20,000 “likely noncitizens” that the Justice Department alleged are on California rolls just last week, and an even tinier fraction of the more than 190,000 noncitizens the Trump administration alleged were on state rolls as recently as July. State officials have previously warned — along with independent elections experts — that the Trump administration has badly overstated voter fraud claims in other states — including in Nevada, where officials recently found that all 185 people the Justice Department flagged as potential noncitizens were in fact citizens — and repeatedly revised downward its estimate for how many “likely noncitizens” are on California’s rolls. Acting Deputy Atty. Gen. Trent McCotter cast the arrests during a Monday news conference as proof that California voter rolls are corrupted and need to be purged to prevent noncitizens from negating the legitimate votes of U.S. citizens, and that California officials who have rebuffed recent Trump administration efforts to purge the state’s rolls are willfully obstructing justice. “This Department of Justice will not look the other way while non-citizens vote in federal elections,” McCotter said. “Unfortunately, the same can’t be said for California and L.A. County.” State and local officials — some of whom are being sued by the Justice Department over their handling of the broader claims — said voter fraud should be taken seriously, but that isolated cases are not evidence of widespread problems and that any voting allegations from the Trump administration must be viewed with skepticism. Los Angeles County Supervisor Janice Hahn referred to Monday’s arrests as “voter intimidation and a blatant attempt to undermine trust in our midterm elections.” “These arrests are being used to paint a picture of widespread voter fraud when we know that is not the case,” Hahn said. “California has laws in place to protect the integrity of our elections, and LA County is fully abiding by them.” California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta’s office said the 28 individuals charged Monday “represent a tiny fraction” of California’s 23 million registered voters, and that the Trump administration has not shown “evidence of widespread voter fraud, even if the allegations are true.” Read more: Big assertions, sharp exchanges, little clarity define DOJ election battle with California Shifting claims For months, federal prosecutors have been issuing grand jury subpoenas for voter records in California — suggesting a sweeping criminal investigation was underway. In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin asserted in a letter to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber that California may have more than 190,000 noncitizen voters on its rolls. Last week, McCotter wrote letters to Weber and Dean Logan, head of the L.A. County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk’s office, giving them 48 hours to set aside the ballots of about 20,000 voters the Justice Department said were “likely noncitizens.” When Weber and Logan balked at the demand — arguing the Justice Department had provided no proof the voters were ineligible, had presented similar and inaccurate claims in other states and had made the request too close to the upcoming election — the Justice Department sued Thursday, asking a court to immediately intervene and force the state and L.A. County to comply with McCotter’s demands. In a filing in that case Monday, federal authorities cited the latest charges as more reason for the court to intervene, and before the election, to segregate out the flagged ballots until those voters’ citizenship can be verified — again raising uncertainty as to their citizenship status despite alleging during their press conference Monday that all were permanent residents. “This Court should order California to set aside vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the federal election — including any ballots cast by the individuals charged with [federal election] crimes this morning — until the voter’s citizenship status can be determined,” federal attorneys wrote. The Trump administration’s apparent uncertainty about the citizenship of the voters it has flagged — and even those it’s charged — has been a focus of state and local officials. Bonta and others have questioned the drop from 190,000 to 20,000 and repeatedly pointed to what occurred in Nevada, where federal officials initially flagged more than 15,000 potential noncitizen voters. Independent election experts have also highlighted those discrepancies. Rick Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at UCLA School of Law, wrote online Monday that the data the federal government relies on to find purported noncitizens is “unreliable.” He wrote that the Justice Department’s demands on California risk “disenfranchising thousands of voters, and from DOJ’s track record, the lion’s share will be eligible voters.” David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, said the 28 alleged noncitizens charged repesent “.0001% of California voters,” and that the Trump administration charging 28 people days after flagging 20,000 “raises serious questions as to whether DOJ has any evidence at all supporting their claims on the other 19,972 on their list.” McCotter said the original 190,000 figure was “the ceiling,” while “20,000 is the floor” — with the larger figure representing individuals the administration had low, medium or high levels of confidence were noncitizens, and the smaller figure representing only those it has high confidence are noncitizens. “So there’s not inconsistency between those numbers. They’re just looking at different levels of confidence,” he said. He also said the notion that a federal list of more than 15,000 alleged noncitizens in Nevada had resulted in zero noncitizens being found was a “false storyline,” in part because the larger group was never vetted by the state. However, he also acknowledged that the 185 that were vetted — and found to be citizens — were those the federal government had held “high confidence” in being noncitizens. How the Justice Department further zeroed in on the 28 charged individuals also was not entirely clear. U.S. Atty. Craig Missakian, the top federal prosecutor in Northern California, said prosecutors compared information from Homeland Security to voter information they subpoenaed from Weber’s office and various county election offices. Some of the criminal complaints said Homeland Security Investigations received investigative referrals from its Identity and Benefit Fraud Unit, which provided “relevant information regarding alleged voter fraud or related identity-based fraud indicators.” Kevin Murphy, special agent in charge of Homeland Security Investigations in San Diego, said the underlying investigations not “based on assumptions or a single piece of information,” but required “thorough investigative work, coordination, and a commitment to ensuring that enforcement action is supported by the facts.” Those charged include 13 people from the Central District of California, who live in Los Angeles, Long Beach, Rancho Palos Verdes, Anaheim, West Covina and other cities. They hail from a mix of nations, including Belize, Canada, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India and Mexico. Five others were charged in the Northern District of California, with one from San Francisco and others from the wider Bay Area; four in the Southern District and six in the Eastern District. Read more: Justice Dept. sues California, seeks to stop state from counting 20,000 ballots First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in L.A., dismissed the idea that such fraud is rare or that Trump officials are overstating the threat. “This is not a conspiracy theory,” Essayli said. “This is not made-up stuff.” Essayli specifically highlighted the case of a 72-year-old from Belize arrested in a pre-dawn raid Monday at his home in Commerce. Federal authorities allege that he fraudulently registered to vote in 2019, voted in 2020, twice in 2022 and again in 2024. He is also accused of lying on his naturalization application. McCotter said in the last seven weeks, the Trump administration has charged 113 people across 20 states with voting-related crimes. More than 154 million people voted nationally in the 2024 presidential election. What’s ahead Federal officials said their work — dubbed “Operation Protect the Vote” — would continue through the election and beyond. Essayli said California’s own process for verifying voters’ citizenship, including requiring that they attest to being a citizen when they register, is insufficient. He said California election officials have “no idea who is a citizen,” but also know “they have noncitizens who are getting ballots as we speak” and several years ago admitted in an audit that noncitizens were being registered at the DMV. “When we submit a list of 20,000 noncitizens to California that we are pretty sure are not citizens, it is outrageous that the response from the state is, ‘We don’t believe you and we’re not even going to look at it,’” he said. “That is not good faith actors. They are being complicit.” McCotter said there “may be some names” on the list of 20,000 flagged voters “who, it turns out, ultimately are citizens.” He said federal authorities are “not perfect,” which is why they’ve asked California officials to work with them. “We could knock through most of these names pretty quickly, probably in a day or two, if California would work with us.” He said the timeline — amid an ongoing election — was due to state officials refusing to cooperate sooner. “It’s an emergency of their own creation.” Sign up for Essential California for news, features and recommendations from the L.A. Times and beyond in your inbox six days a week. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times . item.title: Gun used in Bend school shooting was birthday gift from shooter's mom, sources say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The gun used by a 16-year-old who shot and killed three children and a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, last week was a birthday gift from the shooter's mom, sources told CBS News. The Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun was purchased legally in August 2026 by Shauntai Nickerson, the mother of Griffin J. John II, and given to him for recreational use, the sources said. In 2020, Nickerson told a local television station that her son, who was 10 years old at the time, had special needs and was struggling with remote learning during the pandemic. She told KTVZ, "It'll be great for my son to get back in there and get the help that he needs with the skilled teachers that he needs to get it from." The shooter initially fired at a passing pickup truck, whose driver made the initial 911 call, before forcing his way into the school by shooting through the glass panes of a set of double doors, police said last week. He then went into the first classroom to the left of those doors, where he killed all four victims and wounded two others. The children killed in the shooting were ages 5, 8 and 11, police said. The teacher who was killed was identified as 25-year-old Megan Lambert. The 5-year-old victim was identified by police and his family as Rhoam Summer. The families of the two other children have not made their names public, Bend police said. Two wounded victims are a 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher. Police said Monday there were a total of nine people — four adults and five children — in the classroom at the time. The shooter was shot and killed by a bystander, 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco , who saw the first shooting with the pickup truck and followed the shooter into the school. Giamanco is a Bend resident with two daughters who attend Silver Rail Elementary School. The suspect was a former student of Silver Rail Elementary, police said. No motive for the attack has been provided. The Bend Police Department said Monday it expected to finish collecting evidence at the school by the end of the day, and would then turn the building back over to the school district. Law enforcement sources previously told CBS News that investigators are combing through the computer, phone, social media, search history and other online activity of the attacker. item.title: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moon
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The spacecraft will head to Mars's larger moon, Phobos [JAXA] A spacecraft has launched from Japan headed for Mars' moon Phobos, where it will attempt to grab some moondust and bring it back to Earth. If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth. The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027. It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed. Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth. "I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said. [BBC] There are only three moons in the inner Solar System: our own Moon, and two around Mars, which are called Phobos and Deimos. Both of these are tiny - Phobos is about 20km (12 miles) across and Deimos is about 10km (six miles) across. They are also irregularly shaped, looking a bit like space potatoes. The MMX spacecraft will study Deimos as it arrives in the Mars neighbourhood, and then will focus on Phobos. It plans to set down a small rover to explore the terrain, though this will be no easy feat. Sara Russell says no one has ever landed a rover on such a small moon. "The moon itself doesn't have very much of its own gravity," she explained. "But it's next to an enormous planet that's got a much higher gravity, and that makes it much harder to get a rover onto the surface." Mars got its moons about 4.5bn years ago - but no one knows how they formed [NASA] The rover will scout out a landing site so that the MMX spacecraft itself can later touch down on Phobos. Once on the surface, it will deploy a robotic arm and two samplers to grab some moon dust. This material will be packed into a small capsule that will return to Earth in 2031, landing in the Woomera desert of South Australia. The amount of material that will come back is tiny - just 10g. "It's a very small [amount] actually," said Dr Chrysa Avdellidou, from Leicester University, who is working with the Japanese mission. "However we can do several studies even on individual grains… You don't need to have kilos back from a surface in order to do science. So it's worth every gram," she said. The spacecraft will collect 10g of moon dust from the surface of Phobos [JAXA] Scientists believe the sample will finally shed light on the puzzle of where Mars's moons came from. There are two competing ideas. Either a space rock smashed into Mars early in its history, and Phobos and Deimos were created from the debris. Or the moons are two wandering asteroids from the outer Solar System, which were grabbed by the Red Planet's gravity. "When we get the sample back, we'll be able to look in detail at its chemistry and its mineral composition - and the two hypotheses will produce very distinct results," said Sara Russell. "It should be pretty much immediately obvious.. whether it's the product of this dramatic impact or whether it's a captured asteroid. So we'll find that out really quickly." The team is also hoping there might be an extra bonus coming back to their labs. "One of the really exciting things is that Phobos is so close to the Mars surface that whenever there's an impact into the Mars surface, little grains might actually become implanted into Phobos itself," said Russell. "And that means that the sample we get back may actually contain grains of Mars as well. So it can give us really direct information about the composition and history of Mars." Martian meteorites are rare - this one is on display at the Natural History Museum [Kevin Church/BBC News] Bringing material from Mars back to Earth has long been an ambition of space scientists. The Nasa Perseverance rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, has been carefully collecting samples on Mars and storing them in canisters. But a second Nasa/ESA mission, called Mars Sample Return, that would have picked up and returned these canisters, has been effectively cancelled, after its funding was halted by the US Congress. China is planning its own sampling mission to Mars, set to launch in 2028. It will attempt to return Martian material to Earth in 2031. We do already have some fragments of the Red Planet here on Earth in the form of Martian meteorites. These are pieces of Mars that were blasted off the surface by asteroid strikes, and ended up being hurled towards the Earth. Martian meteorites are extremely rare, but like all space rocks that fall to our planet, they become contaminated as soon as they get here, mixing with the air, dust, soil and water. Scientists are so desperate to get their gloved hands on a direct sample from Mars and its moons because it would be pristine. item.title: Mass. GOP candidate for lieutenant governor suspends campaign after arrest
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The former Massachusetts lieutenant governor-hopeful who was arrested in connection with drunken driving on Saturday night appeared in New Bedford court on Monday morning. Shawn Oliver, 42, is facing charges of operating under the influence (OUI) of alcohol in addition to motor vehicles charges of negligent operation, marked lanes violation and speeding, according to charging documents in his case. Oliver pleaded not guilty and was ordered released on personal recognizance from New Bedford District Court on Monday morning by Judge Joseph Harrington Jr. He is scheduled to appear again on Nov. 16. Oliver is a current New Bedford city councilor and Bristol County House of Corrections officer who was running on the ticket as a Republican candidate with Mike Minogue against current Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll and Gov. Maura Healey. He announced he was suspending his campaign at around 2 p.m. on Sunday, less than 24 hours after his arrest Saturday night and after Minogue had called on him to do so Sunday morning. Read more: The Mass. GOP’s lieutenant governor candidate suspended his campaign. Here’s what’s next “After careful reflection, I have made the decision to suspend my campaign for Lieutenant Governor,” Oliver, who was running as a Republican in the race, said in a statement released at 2:17 p.m. on Sunday. “This election is too important to be overshadowed by personal matters. I want to sincerely thank everyone who has supported me throughout this journey and ask that my family’s privacy be respected during this difficult time,” Oliver said. Oliver’s attorney could not immediately be reached for comment Monday. What happened? According to three New Bedford police reports on the incident, Oliver was driving a black Lincoln Navigator north on Dartmouth Street at around 11:30 p.m., just south of the Rockdale Avenue intersection. A witness who spoke to officers at the scene said he was stopped in his own car behind Oliver’s Navigator at an intersection light on Dartmouth Street. When the light turned green, the witness said the Navigator did not pull forward. After a few moments sitting at the light — and the witness reversing his own car to view that the light was green — the Navigator suddenly accelerated forward and drifted to the right, almost hitting the curb by New York Bagel at 571 Dartmouth St., the report read. The Navigator then “abruptly” veered to the left to avoid striking the curb, the report read, and continued onward. After crossing through the Dartmouth and Rockdale intersection, the Navigator again drifted to the left and crossed over the yellow center line. Police say Oliver struck five parked cars and was driving so fast that he flipped his Navigator upside down onto its roof. Oliver was outside of the car and standing on the sidewalk, speaking on his cellphone when officers arrived at the scene, the report read. A bystander brought out a chair and officers told Oliver to sit down, noting that he was bleeding from an injury on the right side of his head. Oliver repeatedly asked officers at the scene if “everyone else was OK,” though they told him he was the only person involved in the crash, the report read. Oliver also told officers he was “burning both ends of the wick,” and said he “was coming from a meeting with friends in Dartmouth.” Oliver was unable to complete a field sobriety test due to his injuries and was brought to the hospital, where he then told officers he’d drank at least two alcoholic beverages earlier in the night at Black Bass Grill. He then had gone to a friend’s house located in Dartmouth, police said. Oliver’s eyes were “bloodshot and glassy,” he was emanating “a moderate odor of alcoholic beverages” and he vomited at the hospital before he was placed under arrest. “After speaking with Shawn, it was determined that he was under the influence of alcoholic beverages therefore should not have been operating a motor vehicle,” the report read. “At this point he was advised that he was being placed under arrest and was handcuffed to the hospital bed,” the report read. Oliver refused to have his blood drawn at the hospital. item.description:

The Mississippi Attorney General's Office said in a statement on Monday that the Senatobia Police Department was justified in its use of force during a police-involved shooting last June that led to the death of a 1-year-old. Kohen Wiley was shot and killed outside of a Walmart in Senatobia, Mississippi, on June 14 after an officer fired into a vehicle when those in the vehicle were allegedly evading police. The attorney general's office said in its statement on Monday, "In this incident, the Attorney General's Office found the use of force was justified." WATN - PHOTO: Attorney Ben Crump, at podium, is joined by members of Kohen Wiley's family during a press event in Senatobia, Mississippi, June 22, 2026. In a statement released in September by Senatobia Interim Chief of Police Angelica Maze, the Mississippi Bureau of Investigations handed its investigative findings into Wiley's death to the Mississippi Attorney General's office, as required by law. The shooting occurred after law enforcement officers responded to a shoplifting call in Senatobia, according to the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation. Officers who responded to a shoplifting call encountered two adults allegedly fleeing from the store with a child and going into a vehicle, according to the bureau. Attorneys for the Wiley family said that the adults were accused of stealing diapers. WATN - PHOTO: Photos of Kohen Wiley are shown during a press event in Senatobia, Mississippi, June 22, 2026. Officers attempted to stop the vehicle, with one opening fire when the driver allegedly drove toward them, the bureau said. The child was killed and an adult critically injured, officials said. item.title: Tensions flare at court hearing on Trump's D.C. golf course renovation
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Golfers play past felled trees at East Potomac Golf Links in Washington D.C., US, on Sunday. - Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg/Getty Images One of the tensest showdowns between the Trump administration and the federal bench in Washington, DC, came to a head on Monday in a marathon court hearing over the President Donald Trump’s efforts to overhaul a golf course that has been the subject of months of litigation. Trump early Monday doubled down on his plan to close and renovate a public Washington, DC, golf course , saying construction would begin “IMMEDIATELY” despite a judge’s order to provide three days’ notice ahead of any construction. Trump wrote in a Truth Social post that the government does not “need an approval” to proceed with the construction. “Work is scheduled to begin IMMEDIATELY! The finished product will be World Class, and bring income and great prestige back to D.C.,” he wrote. But his plan to renovate the East Potomac Golf Course is already the subject of a legal fight as preservationists and golfers seek to stop the president from changing the public park. The case may seem relatively minor compared to some of the other sweeping legal battles of Trump’s second term. But the litigation has demanded the attention of several top attorneys from the Justice Department, who have sought to defend the actions government officials who are overseeing the course and have tried distinguish them from the president’s public statements about his intentions for the grounds. US District Judge Ana C. Reyes, who is overseeing the case, issued an order last week that requires the government to give at least three days’ notice before making any “irreparable modification” to the course. Reyes and the third-highest ranking Justice Department official, Associate Attorney General Stan Woodward, sparred repeatedly over the information she was demanding from the administration. The question in the case, since last Monday, had largely been about the administration removing, with less of a day’s notice to the court, of 400-plus trees from the park earlier this month. But the hearing on Monday quickly turned into a clash over what Trump wrote on social media, the Justice Department’s ability to defend separate assertions made by the National Park Service in court, and how far the federal trial-level court can go to demand answers from the executive branch. “I don’t know what to do, when I keep getting different stories,” Reyes told Woodward as the hearing began with a heated moment. “I have, on the one hand the president of the United States saying to the American people … there is a final plan,” Reyes said hours later in the same hearing Monday. “I have you all telling me, witnesses saying what they’re saying, there is no final plan … which is it?” Robert Stander – a DOJ attorney who was handling the bulk of the administration’s legal arguments – struggled to answer the question directly and Reyes rejected his attempts to compare the social media posts to an executive order that was just the start of an agency’s work on a project, rather than a final decision. Woodward returned to the line of questioning at the end of the hearing and told Reyes there was “no plan to close the course, as those words have their literal meaning.” He told the judge that asking Stander, a lower-level attorney that did not go through Senate confirmation, to contradict the president put his colleague in a “difficult” position. Reyes is considering whether to issue a longer-term order limiting what the administration can do to the course, including cutting down more trees. Last week, Reyes presided over a testy hearing in which she said she was “furious” with the administration for removing hundreds of trees without proper notice. The government claimed the removals were routine maintenance unrelated to any plan to renovate the golf course. Reyes ordered that no more trees be cut down before October 26. The Justice Department on Friday filed a motion asking for Reyes’ removal from the case , accusing her of having a “disdain for the Trump Administration.” Reyes over the weekend denied that motion and refuted the government’s claims against her. In his Monday post to Truth Social, Trump disparaged Reyes a “crazed lunatic.” The golf course is one of several renovation projects Trump is working on in Washington. The president’s desire to turn the public course into a professional course – a renovation that could cost between $20 million and $49 million – has angered those who fear it may take away a public and affordable place to play golf in the nation’s capital. Administration officials express ignorance to Trump’s intentions Amid the tense exchanges between DOJ and the judge were hours of testimony from government officials charged with oversight of federal public grounds – testimony that turned the proceedings into a grueling drag through bureaucratic procedures of the National Park Service. Multiple government officials who oversee the golf course expressed ignorance to Trump’s latest assertions about the future of the course. The acting director of the National Park Service, Jessica Bowron – who signed off on this month’s move to cut down the 400-plus trees – said she was not aware of plans to close East Potomac Park next month, nor had she been in any discussions about renovating the course. She and other officials say their work on the removing the trees was carried out under a directive that they implement recommendations from 2019 for making the course look more it did when it was first built, in a proposal known as the Cultural Landscape Report. Reyes has said that she believed that explanation was a pretext for giving the administration cover to start the renovation. She quizzed officials Monday on the “coincidence” that the administration suddenly rushed to implement a seven-year-old proposal – specifically, only its recommendations to cut down certain trees – just as Trump was demanding work on his overhaul to begin. Greg Wischer – a political appointee at the Interior Department who has coordinated Trump’s directives for “beautifying” Washington, DC – testified that he came across of 2019 landscape recommendations as part of research in recent months for what his agency could do to “clean up” the course. He suggested that those “clean up” efforts were separate from the Trump-ordered redesign. DOJ assertions of privilege prevented him from answering several questions about key meetings and conversations that preceded the tree removals. But his testimony revealed that for months he has been receiving “conceptual proposals” for renovating the course from famed golf course designer Tom Fazio and his son Gavin. Wischer first saw the rendering posted by Trump on Sunday last week, according to his testimony, when Gavin Fazio texted it to his personal phone. Later in the hearing, Reyes asked Stander whether there was a contract with the Fazios to redo the course and asked the other attorneys at the defense table when Stander said he did not know the answer.
